objective: Choose page-level landmark elements over div soup so assistive technology exposes navigable regions.
defects: hint is the generic shape-based fallback
explanation only refutes the class-name distractor and never says why a `section` per region fails, which is the interesting case

rewrite.hint: Ask which of these the browser exposes as page regions a screen-reader user can jump to, rather than which ones you can style.
rewrite.explanation: At page level `header`, `nav`, `main`, `aside` and `footer` are exposed as banner, navigation, main, complementary and contentinfo landmarks, so a screen reader can list them and move between them. Class names and ids are never exposed to assistive technology. A `section` is only exposed as a `region` when it has an accessible name, so a bare `section` per region maps to `generic` and adds nothing.

rationale: Correct, well-pitched opener for the level objective; only the filler hint and the unaddressed `section` distractor fall short.
evidence: https://www.w3.org/TR/html-aria/ : header -> banner and footer -> contentinfo when not nested in article/aside/main/nav/section; nav -> navigation; main -> main; aside -> complementary; section -> region only with an accessible name, otherwise generic

cs.notes: Czech asks "Co znamena zkratka HTML?" with four expansion options; a translation of the older abbreviation-style bank, unrelated to the English landmark question.

objective: Explain why a document has at most one main and what a second one costs a landmark user.
defects: distractor 3 ("It is required for the page to validate") is factually true: the spec forbids more than one non-hidden main, so a conformance checker does flag it
hint is the generic shape-based fallback
explanation never says that browsers do render a second main, which is what makes distractor 0 tempting

options: Browsers refuse to render a second one
`main` marks the page's primary content, and two of them means neither is primary
CSS cannot target more than one
Search engines rank a page with two of them lower
rewrite.hint: Think about what a skip-to-content link, or a list of landmarks, has to point at when two regions both claim to be the main one.
rewrite.explanation: `main` names the one region holding this page's own content, so a skip link and a landmark list have a single unambiguous target; two of them make that choice meaningless. Nothing is enforced at runtime — a browser renders the second one and CSS still matches both — but the spec does forbid more than one non-hidden `main`, so a conformance checker reports it.

rationale: The objective is sound but the fourth option is a true statement, so two options answer the question as asked. Replacing that distractor and naming the validation fact in the explanation fixes it.
evidence: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/grouping-content.html : "A document must not have more than one main element that does not have the hidden attribute specified."
https://www.w3.org/TR/html-aria/ : main -> role=main

cs.notes: Czech asks "K cemu se HTML pouziva?" (what HTML is used for) with styling/structure/interactivity options; a different, older question.

objective: Read heading levels as document structure rather than text size, and see what skipping a level claims.
defects: distractor 2 ("The page fails to validate") is uncomfortably close to true: the current spec requires each heading to be at most one level deeper than the previous one, even though MDN frames skipping as an accessibility problem and the W3C checker does not report it
hint is the generic shape-based fallback

options: The visual size of the heading
The document outline: a reader navigating by heading level sees two missing levels
The `h4` stops being announced as a heading
Search engines refuse to index it
rewrite.hint: Heading elements carry a level, and someone navigating by level reads levels as nesting. Ask what the jump from 1 to 4 claims about this page.
rewrite.explanation: Heading elements carry level, not size, so `h1` followed by `h4` tells anyone navigating by heading that two levels of nesting sit in between when they do not exist. The `h4` is still announced as a heading — only its level is wrong — and the size it renders at is CSS's job, not the element's.

rationale: Key and explanation are right and the objective is core to the level; the validation distractor is contestable under the current spec text and should be replaced.
evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/Heading_Elements : "Do not skip heading levels", framed as an accessibility problem; "Do not use heading elements to resize text. Instead, use the CSS font-size property"

https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/sections.html : "Each heading following another heading lead in the outline must have a heading level that is less than, equal to, or 1 greater than lead's heading level."

objective: Know what the lang attribute actually changes: language-dependent rendering and speech, not direction or encoding.
defects: hint is the generic shape-based fallback
explanation covers only the speech half and leaves the dir, charset and browser-UI distractors unanswered

rewrite.hint: Ask which of these depends on knowing which language the text is in — not on how the file is encoded or which way it reads.
rewrite.explanation: `lang` tags the language of the content, so a screen reader selects the matching voice and pronunciation rules and the browser can hyphenate with the right dictionary — `hyphens: auto` does nothing without it. Direction comes from `dir`, encoding from `meta charset`, and the browser's own interface language is a user setting a page cannot change.

rationale: Directly relevant to a bilingual product and correctly keyed; the distractors are good enough that the explanation should refute them rather than stop at the voice.
evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Global_attributes/lang : "to allow assistive technologies such as screen readers to invoke the correct pronunciation"; required for WCAG 3.1.1/3.1.2

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/hyphens : "Hyphenation rules are language-specific. In HTML, the language is determined by the lang attribute. Browsers will only hyphenate if this attribute is present"

cs.notes: Czech asks which comment syntax is valid HTML; an older question with no relation to the lang attribute.

objective: Recognise that section only carries region semantics when it has an accessible name.
defects: conflates "no heading" with "no accessible name": a heading inside a section does not name it unless aria-labelledby points at it
explanation rests on the document outline, which the spec's outline algorithm no longer provides; the real mechanism is the role mapping
distractor 3 refers to a "validation score", which does not exist
hint is the generic shape-based fallback

rewrite.question: A `section` has no accessible name — no `aria-label`, no `aria-labelledby`. What is it doing for a reader?
options: Exposing a named region a screen reader can jump to
Very little — without a name it is exposed as a generic container, like a `div`
Making the content focusable for keyboard users
Grouping the content as a separate document for search engines
rewrite.hint: Ask what a screen reader can announce about this container, and what would have to be present for it to be a region at all.
rewrite.explanation: A `section` maps to the `region` landmark only when it has an accessible name; without one it maps to `generic`, which is exactly what a `div` maps to. The fix is to name it — usually `aria-labelledby` pointing at the heading inside it — because a heading sitting in a section does not name the section on its own.

rationale: The point is worth teaching but the premise is imprecise: it is the accessible name, not the heading, that decides the mapping. Restating the question and explanation around the name keeps the objective and makes it correct.
evidence: https://www.w3.org/TR/html-aria/ : "Section elements only map to role=region if the element has an accessible name"; otherwise role=generic
https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/sections.html : "The section element is not a generic container element"; a section is "a thematic grouping of content, typically with a heading"

cs.notes: Czech asks which file extension HTML files use; an older question with no relation to section semantics.

objective: Separate document metadata in head from rendered content in body, and know why encoding must come early.
defects: hint is the generic shape-based fallback
explanation says "declared late" without the concrete rule (the declaration must be inside the first 1024 bytes)

rewrite.hint: Ask what the browser needs to know about the document before it can render any of it.
rewrite.explanation: `head` carries metadata about the document — title, encoding, viewport, stylesheet links — while a heading, navigation and a footer are content the reader sees, so they belong in `body`. Encoding is the urgent one: the declaration has to sit within the first 1024 bytes, because by the time the parser has read further it has already had to guess how to decode the bytes.

rationale: A simple sorting question, but a foundation the rest of the level rests on and correctly keyed. The 1024-byte rule turns a vague explanation into something checkable.
evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/meta : charset "declares the document's character encoding" and such meta elements "must be located entirely within the first 1024 bytes of the document"

rewrite.explanation: Submitting is an action on the current page, not a navigation, so a link makes a promise the control does not keep — and an `a` with no `href` is not even focusable. A `<button>` inside a form defaults to `type="submit"`, so it submits with no handler at all, and it responds to Enter and Space as a button.

rationale: Correct and verified, but it earns its place next to rm-html-9 only through the default submit type, so the explanation should state that outright.
evidence: node: jsdom, <button id="btn">go</button> inside a form -> btn.type === "submit"
https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/button : submit is "the default if the attribute is not specified for buttons associated with a <form>"

the item asks what else changes but never mentions that browsers now imply rel="noopener" for target="_blank", which is the other thing that changed

options: Nothing else changes
The new tab starts with no history, so Back is no longer the way out
The link stops being reachable from the keyboard
The visited state is no longer applied to it
rewrite.hint: The new tab is a fresh browsing context. Ask what the user had in the old one that they no longer have.
rewrite.explanation: A new tab starts with no session history, so Back no longer returns the user to where they were, which is why MDN advises saying in the link text when a link opens a new tab. It changes neither focusability nor the visited state, and modern browsers already imply `rel="noopener"` for `target="_blank"`, so that is no longer something you add by hand.

rationale: The objective is right and the key is the only true option, but it is phrased as advice and the item silently skips the noopener change that is the other half of the answer.
evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/a : "Setting target=\"_blank\" on <a> elements implicitly provides the same rel behavior as setting rel=\"noopener\""; links opening a new tab "should indicate what will happen when the link is followed"

rewrite.question: What does `blockquote` with a `cite` attribute express?
rewrite.hint: One part marks the words as somebody else's; the other records where they came from. Neither is a font style.
rewrite.explanation: `blockquote` marks the content as quoted from elsewhere and the `cite` attribute holds the URL of the source. That attribute is machine-readable only — browsers do not display it — so visible attribution goes beside the quote, usually in a `cite` element outside the blockquote. Italic text is styling and says nothing about where the words came from.

rationale: The weakest keeper in the batch: the objective is legitimate but narrow, and the cite attribute is invisible to users, which the item should say rather than imply it is useful attribution.

rewrite.hint: Enter does not submit the form directly — it presses something first. Ask what it presses.
rewrite.explanation: Enter in a text field clicks the form's default button, the first submit button in the form. Replace that button with a `div` and a click handler and the mouse path keeps working while the keyboard path disappears silently, which is why a keyboard pass finds bugs a mouse pass cannot. The exception is worth knowing: with no submit button at all, Enter still submits a form that has only one field blocking implicit submission, but does nothing once there is more than one.

rationale: The key is right and the symptom is a real one, but the explanation states a rule the spec does not have, so a learner would draw the wrong conclusion about single-field forms.
evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLFormElement/submit_event : "the browser fires a click event at that button. The default button is the first submit button in tree order whose form owner is that form"; "if the form has no submit button and more than one input blocking implicit submission, the gesture never triggers implicit submission"
